Distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, NGO representatives, let me start by welcoming you all to the 2026 regular session of the Committee. I'm deeply honored to be elected to serve as the Chair of the Committee on Non-Governmental Organizations. But as we approach the UN's 80th anniversary, a milestone that changes every part of the system to deliver better, we also know that incremental adjustments will not be enough. The world has changed dramatically since the resolution of 1996/31 was adopted. The scale, diversity, and sophistication of NGO engagement have outgrown our current working methods. If we want to maintain the credibility and effectiveness of this mechanism, if we want to support member states rather than slow them down, we must together embrace a more ambitious spirit of renewal. Our goal is straightforward: a committee that is more transparent, more predictable, more accessible for applicants, and more efficient for delegations. That means streamlining repetitive procedures, using digital tools where they add clarity and speed, and supporting NGOs to provide timely, high-quality information. It also means clear, even-handed time management in the room. This begins with tackling the growing backlog of deferred applications and reports. Today we have before us 237 new applications, 381 deferred applications, which makes a whopping 618 in total, 773 quadrennial reports, and 154 deferred reports from 100 organizations. This is a significant workload. It underscores why modernizing our working methods is not an abstract exercise but a practical necessity. To ensure we can complete our work on time, I propose that we allocate 1 minute for each new application and 2 minutes for each deferred application, and that we adhere strictly to the programme of work agreed by the Committee. In this spirit, I will work with the Bureau, with all Committee members during the informal working group to accelerate these reforms, drawing on your ideas and experience to develop changes that modernise and improve our Committee. I also want to warmly, warmly welcome representatives of NGOs joining us in person and online. Creating opportunities for meaningful Engagement by civil society at the global, regional, and national levels is essential to advancing the implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals and safeguard the progress that has been achieved through decades of efforts in core development areas of health, education, gender equality, human rights, and so on. Civil society brings invaluable knowledge, expertise, innovation, and practical solutions that are critical to addressing today's complex global challenges. They are part of solutions while also contributing to holding actors accountable, and their space is shrinking in our increasingly unpredictable and tumultuous world. This is deeply concerning. Through the committee's consideration of applications for consultative status and making recommendations, NGOs are enabled to participate actively in ECOSOC's subsidiary bodies, other ECOSOC fora, and the wider work of the United Nations, hereby safeguarding their access to the UN system. Before closing, I would like to draw the Committee's attention to the impact of the UN current financial situation and its direct implications on the operational capacity of our Office. The NGO Branch has seen an 88% increase in applications for presentation by the Committee in the last 10 years, to now nearly 1,200 for the 2026 cycle. This is a welcome increase and speaks to the interest of NGOs to be part of the UN and the global conversation. We now have more than 6,700 accredited NGOs. Just to give an example of the type of work in the back, our review of quadrennial reports have increased to over 1,200 in 2025 alone. There is a real risk that the NGO Branch may eventually be unable to fully support the Committee in accordance in accordance with mandate of ECOSOC Resolution 1996/31. Thank you, Chair, and let me begin by joining the previous speaker in congratulating both you and your Vice Chair on your election, and joining you also in expressing appreciation for the efforts of the NGO branch in organizing this session. The United Kingdom remains dedicated to upholding civic space and fundamental freedoms, both globally and within the UN framework. Civil society organizations are essential contributors to advancing sustainable development, to defending human rights, addressing a range of challenges from climate change to conflict, and of course holding leaders accountable. When civil society can engage freely and securely without interference, and society as a whole benefits from their crucial input and factual evidence. This is particularly vital as we work to strengthen the UN's ability to respond to the complex shared challenges we face worldwide. Regrettably, these positive contributions are not acknowledged everywhere, and there are ongoing efforts by a limited group of Member States to obstruct or postpone the involvement of legitimate NGOs. Tactics such as politically driven questioning, repeated postponements, and improper use of procedural rules undermine trust in this committee and result in unnecessary delays. Such actions contradict both the intention and the principles enshrined in ECOSOC Resolution 1996/31, which aims to encourage, not inhibit, genuine collaboration between civil society and member states. The UK remains committed to supporting the accreditation of all bona fide NGOs. Consistent with Resolution 1996/31, our evaluations will focus strictly on 4 criteria: that the NGO is actively engaged and functioning; that the NGO operates independently of government control; that the NGO does not inflict harm on individuals, property, or the environment; and that the NGO and its personnel adhere to the UN Charter and refrain from politically motivated attacks or profiting from illegal activities. As we commence this session, the United Kingdom encourages all committee members to review NGO applications with impartiality, with consistency, and with a collective commitment to fostering a secure, inclusive, and supportive environment for civil society within the United Nations.

Thank you, Chair. At the outset of this session, the European Union and its member states thank the Chair and all the members of the Committee for undertaking this important responsibility, and we also express our appreciation for the important work of the NGO branch. The EU reaffirms its unwavering commitment to a diverse, adequately resourced, and independent civil society. Meaningful civil society engagement is not peripheral to the United Nations. It's integral to the organization's capacity to deliver on its mandate and to translate global commitments into tangible impacts on the ground. Across development, peacebuilding, and human rights, civil society society organizations bridge the gap between international norms and lived realities, ensuring that UN decisions extend beyond conference rooms and reach the communities they are intended to serve. Despite a context of steadily narrowing civic space globally, the strength and credibility of multilateral deliberations depend in no small measure on an openness to hearing independent voices regardless of potential differences of opinion. As a subsidiary body of ECOSOC, the NGO Committee has a clear and specific mandate to facilitate, not impede, NGO participation in the work of the UN. In reviewing applications for consultative status, the Committee must be guided solely by the general interest and by fully respecting the letter and spirit of the ECOSOC Resolution Resolution 1996/31. The EU remains concerned by the continued and unjustified deferrals of some NGO applications, in many cases over multiple years, on basis of dubious arguments and repetitive questions, contrary to the spirit of Resolution 1996/31. Such practices risk undermining confidence in the UN's engagement with civil society at a moment when trust in multilateral institutions is already under significant strain. For this session, the EU sees no justification for further delaying the consideration of long-pending applications of a number of EU-based NGOs, as well as by organizations from other regions of the world, that have been unjustifiably pending for a long time. We therefore urge the Committee to act with the responsibility and resolve, and to grant consultative status to eligible organizations without further undue delay. Reform of the NGO Committee is both timely and necessary. In the context of ongoing UNAID reform efforts and a persistent liquidity crisis, enhancing the efficiency, transparency, and predictability of the Committee's work is not merely desirable, it's essential. A more effective accreditation process is a concrete and cost-efficient means of strengthening the UN's delivery capacity and institutional credibility. In this regard, the EU also underscores the importance of robust and inclusive working modalities. The potential for hybrid participation to enhance equitable access, particularly for civil society actors, from conflict-affected or resource-constrained settings, and to improve the efficiency of the Committee's work, merits serious and thoughtful consideration as part of a holistic and comprehensive approach to the Committee's reform. In conclusion, the EU and its member states stand ready to engage constructively with all members of the Committee and address outstanding challenges, and to act in the shared interest of an inclusive, effective, and credible United Nations. We wish you all a productive and successful session. Thank you.

Mr. Chair, in the beginning, Algeria wishes to reaffirm its appreciation for the vital role NGOs play in supporting the activities of ECOSOC and other UN subsidiary bodies. We may disagree with the content of some NGO statements, but we believe it is essential that civil society views be openly heard in UN fora. While we respect the diversity of civil society voices, we must emphasize that consultative status is a privilege governed by ECOSOC Resolution 1996/31. As stipulated in paragraphs 55 and 57 of this resolution, NGOs must conform at all times to the principles underpinning the establishment and nature of their consultative relations. In instances where clear evidence of non-compliance with ECOSOC status occurs, this committee has a duty to review the organization's status to prevent further abuse of the system. Mr. Chair, we would like to raise the case of 2 NGOs, namely Il Cenacolo and Comité International pour le Respect et l'Application de la Charte Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples, or CIHRAC. Regarding the NGO Il Cenacolo, we have identified the following. First, while its official ICESO profile lists the organization as Italy-based with a local geographic scope, we were unable to verify its existence on the official registry of Italian NGOs. Second, the 2 most recent quadriennial reports of this NGO claim it is a completely self-financing entity with more than 800 members. Across 5 continents. The lack of any fluctuation in membership figures over 2 reporting cycles raises questions regarding the accuracy and transparency of the organization's reporting. Third, the NGO has moved beyond its declared expertise in education and youth to intervene in issues such as humanitarian affairs and international law, which are fields that exceed its registered mandate. It is further noted that another significant discrepancy exists regarding the organization's foundational identity. While early quadrennial reports identified the NGO as a specialized affiliate of World Health Clinicians focused on women's health, recent filings describe it as a broad cultural organization. This radical shift from a specialized health affiliate to a generalist entity indicates a lack of continuity in its core mandate. By moving beyond its declared expertise in education and youth into the complex realms of international law and humanitarian affairs, the NGO is operating well outside the technical field of competence for which it was originally granted consultative status. Fourth, for exactly 28 sessions of the Human Rights Council, this organization has demonstrated a systematic pattern of politically motivated oral and written statements directed exclusively at a single UN member state. These activities do not represent a constructive contribution to the work of ECOSOC. but rather an exploitation of the consultative platform. Furthermore, the NGO has utilized language that is not in manifest accord with the spirit of the UN Charter and without observing the required decorum. Mr. Chair, we have the following questions and queries addressed to this NGO. First, The organization requested— is requested to share a recent valid legal certification of current registration issued by an Italian governmental authority, along with the list of members of its executive board, as well as its constitutions, charter, and/or status, bylaws, and amendments to those documents. Pursuant to paragraph 10 of ECOSOC Resolution 1996/31? Second, what are the motivations behind intervening in fields beyond the NGO's geographic scope and field of expertise declared in its consultative relation? Can the NGO provide the specific board resolutions or internal governing minutes that authorized this shift in thematic and geographic focus. Third and last, the organization is requested to share the 2 most recent externally audited financial statements and information on its sources of funding. Turning now to, uh, CIRAC. We raise the following concerns. First, while CIRAC's consultative expertise is registered as limited to sustainable development and gender issues, it consistently intervenes on matters far outside its declared consultative relation and expertise. Second, despite its name, which suggests advocacy for the African Charter on Human and People's Rights. This NGO's activities and statements are frequently at odds with the African Charter provisions or exceed the scope of this legally binding treaty. Furthermore, according to the official records examined, the NGO has never actually made a single reference to the provisions of the African Charter in its statements to the Human Rights Council. Third, the Organization has on several occasions delivered interventions that fall outside the scope of the agenda item under consideration. This pattern of behavior has resulted in more than one call to order from various presiding officers, like during the 54th session of the Human Rights Council. Fourth, evidence indicates that some individuals represented Sirak and other organizations during several Human Rights Council sessions. This multiple representation practice, or in other terms, NGO-hopping, raises significant concerns regarding the independence of these entities and the legitimacy of the credentials issued to their representatives. Lastly, credible information indicates that this NGO engages in the unauthorized sale of UN ground passes and speaking slots in Geneva to various individuals, a practice that undermines the integrity of the consultative status and process during the Human Rights Council sessions. Before addressing some questions to CIRAC, I would like to underscore that the case of this NGO is not merely a matter of differing views, but a fundamental breach to the technical requirements set forth in provisions contained in paragraphs 3, 20, 23, and 55 of Resolution 1996/55. First, paragraph 3 and the mandate integrity. This provision stipulates that an NGO must support the UN in accordance with its own aims and purposes. By invoking the African Charter while systematically ignoring its legal provisions, the NGO is in a state of fundamental misalignment. It is effectively operating under under a mandate that differs from the one approved by ECOSOC. Second, paragraph 20 and expertise requirements. Consultative arrangements exist to secure expert information from organizations with special competence. CERAC's consistent interventions in matters far outside its registered expertise represent a dilution of the consultative process. When an NGO provides non-expert advice, it devalues the technical nature of our work. Third, paragraph 23 and status classification. Special status is reserved for NGOs concerned specifically with only a few fields of activity. By acting as a generalist entity with a limitless agenda, CERAC has abandoned the specific basis upon which its status was granted. It no longer meets the definition of special consultative status as established by the Council. Finally, paragraph 55 and systemic compliance. This paragraph mandates the or that NGOs conform at all times to the principles of their consultative relation. This pattern of behavior we have documented, including procedural disruptions and the alleged sale of credentials represent a serious and material breach to or of this permanent obligation. Mr. Chair, we have the following questions and queries addressed to this NGO. First, what are the motivations behind intervening in fields exceeding its geographic scope and thematic expertise declared in its consultative relation with ECOSOC and in its branding name. Can the NGO provide the specific board resolutions or internal governing minutes that authorize this shift in thematic and geographic focus? Second, in light of the documented disconnect between the NGO's activities and the legal provisions of the African Charter, How does the organization justify its ongoing compliance with the obligations under paragraphs 3, 20, 23, and 55 of ECOSOC Resolution 1996/31? Specifically, does the NGO intend to formally amend its founding documents and change its name to accurately reflect its actual thematic and geographic activities. Third, regarding the grave allegations of unauthorized sale of UN ground passes and speaking slots, the NGO is requested to provide a formal clarification of its position on these allegations, along with a detailed description of its criteria and internal process used to select and vet representatives who are not members of the organization. Fourth, the organization is requested to share a recent proof of existence in the 2 countries where it is based, along with its offices' address, a list of its executive board members, and its official record of the current leadership's appointment. Additionally, the organization is requested to share the official list of designated authorized representatives submitted to the UN Secretariat for the 2022-2025 period, as well as the internal board resolutions confirming that these specific individuals have the authority to speak for the organization's members pursuant to paragraph 11 of ECOSOC Resolution 1996/31. Specifically, CIRAC is asked to disclose if any of its leaders or authorized representatives simultaneously hold high-level positions in other NGOs that have ECOSOC status. Fifth and last, the organization is requested to share its 2 most recent externally audited financial statements and information regarding its sources of funding. Before concluding, I wish to draw the attention of colleagues to the fact that we had requested some information regarding these 2 NGOs, including the full consultative status application, prior to this committee session. However, the Secretariat was unable to provide them. Mr. Chair, we remain at the disposal of fellow committee members for any further details or clarification, and I thank you.
